title: The caterpillar’s menu
teaches: How plants defend themselves with poisons, spines and toughness, what defence costs, and how specialist insects beat one family's poisons and use them to find their food

blocks.text: The caterpillar of the cabbage white butterfly eats cabbage, broccoli, kale, mustard, radish, cress and the other plants of the mustard family. Offered lettuce, spinach or almost anything else, it refuses, and if nothing else is offered it starves to death on a full plate. Yet it also eats a few plants that look nothing like a cabbage: garden nasturtiums, capers and mignonette.

It is easy to think of plants as passive, standing still while animals eat them. But a plant can't run, so it does what it can where it stands: most of the leaves around you are tough, prickly, bitter or poisonous, and most of the insects that could eat them don't. The cabbage white's fussiness is one end of a long contest between plants and the animals that eat them.

In 1910 the Dutch botanist Eduard Verschaffelt asked what the cabbage white's plants have in common. Cabbages, nasturtiums and capers belong to different families by their flowers, but they share a group of chemicals: they all make **mustard-oil glucosides**,[^glucosinolates] mustard oils with a sugar attached that keeps them harmless, the source of the sharp taste of mustard, horseradish and wasabi. The leaf stores them harmlessly, along with an enzyme kept in separate cells. When an animal chews the leaf, the two mix and release the sharp, poisonous mustard oils.

Verschaffelt pressed juice from mustard-family plants and smeared it on leaves the caterpillars normally refused. They ate them. The chemical that keeps most insects off a cabbage was, for this one, the signal that it had found food. The butterflies use it the same way: a female cabbage white tastes a leaf with her feet before she lays her eggs on it.

For a long time botanists called chemicals like the mustard oils secondary substances, and some thought they were waste the plant had to store somewhere. In 1959 the entomologist Gottfried Fraenkel argued that they are there for defence: their whole job is to make the plant unpleasant or dangerous to eat. Many of the strongest drugs people use are plant defences: nicotine, caffeine, morphine, and digitalis, the heart drug from foxglove.

Chemistry isn't the only defence. Grass leaves are stiffened with grains of silica, a kind of glass, that wear down teeth. Holly leaves low on a tree, within a deer's reach, are spinier than the ones above. A stinging nettle's hairs are tiny glass needles that break off in the skin and inject an irritating mix. Some plants make more poison only once they are bitten: a wild tobacco plant that is chewed makes several times more nicotine in its leaves within days.[^talking]

None of this is free. The sugar and nitrogen a plant puts into poisons, spines and tough fibres, and the energy it spends hauling silica up from the soil, are not going into new leaves, roots or seeds. So a defence pays only if it saves more than it costs.

blocks.title: Estimate
points: Caterpillars would eat a fifth of an undefended plant's leaves. If growth falls in step with leaf lost, it keeps 80 percent of its growth.

A defence costs a tenth of growth, leaving 90 percent, and leaf eaten still cuts that in step: 90 × (1 − eaten) must beat 80, so less than about 11 percent may be eaten. The defence must save about half the leaf that would have been lost.

blocks.caption: How well a plant grows against how much poison it makes. A model.

blocks.text: A poison keeps off most insects, but not all of them for ever. Among millions of caterpillars, any that happen to tolerate a little more of the mustard oils get a food that their rivals can't touch, and selection does the rest, as with the orchid and its moth in lesson 18. The cabbage white's caterpillars make a protein in their gut that turns the mustard oils into a harmless form before they can do damage.[^gut]

Once an insect can handle one family's poison, the poison becomes a signal, and the insect often stops eating anything else. Surveys of plant-eating insects find that most are specialists like this, feeding on one family or a few. The monarch butterfly's caterpillars eat milkweeds, whose bitter sap poisons the heart, and store the poison in their own bodies, where it stays through the change into a butterfly. In the 1960s Lincoln Brower fed monarchs to blue jays; a jay that ate one vomited within minutes and afterwards avoided monarchs on sight.[^monarch] The milkweed's defence ends up defending the butterfly.

In 1964 Paul Ehrlich, who studied butterflies, and Peter Raven, a botanist, compared which butterfly groups eat which plant families. Their pattern was so regular that they proposed a history for it. A plant lineage hits on a new poison that its eaters can't handle. Freed from them, it spreads into new places and splits into many species. Eventually some insect evolves a way through, and its descendants spread across that whole family of plants in turn. Then some plant hits on another new defence, and it starts again.

blocks.caption: Two sister groups of plants, one with a new poison, over 60 million years. A model.
blocks.task: Try a specialist that comes early and one that comes late

blocks.text: Ehrlich and Raven called this **coevolution**, the word lesson 18 used for the orchid and its moth, and it is still argued how often things happened in that order. But the pattern they saw holds up: the mustard family and its relatives, with their mustard oils, and the cabbage whites and their relatives, which DNA dates to about the same time, some 80 to 90 million years ago, have diversified side by side. Lesson 21 shows that DNA puts the cabbage white's odd menu, of cabbages, capers and nasturtiums, on one branch of the flowering-plant tree.

parts.title: Why the world is green, again

blocks.text: Ecology's lesson 8 asked why plant-eaters haven't eaten the world bare, and followed one answer: their predators hold them down. This lesson is the other half. Most of what is green around you is tough, prickly or poisonous to most of the animals that could eat it, and each eater can handle only a few of those defences. Predators above and defences below are both true at once, in different measure in different places.

Look at the plants in a garden or a park in late summer, and notice which are chewed full of holes and which are untouched. The cabbages and nasturtiums may well be riddled. Don't taste anything to find out why: some of the untouched ones, like foxglove and yew, are poisonous to people too.

blocks.caption: Six questions on plant defence
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: What did Verschaffelt's smeared leaves show?
choices: Cabbage white caterpillars recognise their food by the mustard plants' chemicals
The caterpillars were hungry enough to eat anything
Mustard juice poisons cabbage white caterpillars
items.why: With mustard-family juice smeared on them, leaves the caterpillars normally refused were eaten. The chemical is their signal for food.

items.ask: A caterpillar eats only cabbages, capers and nasturtiums. Which of these is it most likely to eat too?
choices: Horseradish, which tastes sharp with mustard oils
Kale's look-alike, lettuce, grown in the same garden
Potato leaves, which are poisonous to most insects
items.why: Its plants share mustard-oil chemicals, not looks. Horseradish has them; lettuce and potato don't.

items.ask: Why isn't every plant as poisonous as it could possibly be?
choices: Poison costs growth, and past some point it costs more than the leaf it saves
Animals evolve to tolerate any poison at once
The strongest poisons would kill the plant itself
items.why: The sugar and nitrogen put into defence aren't put into growth. Where few animals feed, a cheap defence or none grows best.

items.ask: Why does a blue jay that has eaten a monarch butterfly avoid monarchs afterwards?
choices: The butterfly carried milkweed poison stored as a caterpillar, which made the jay sick
Monarchs are too big for a jay to swallow
Monarchs fly too fast to catch
items.why: Monarch caterpillars store the milkweed's heart poison. Lincoln Brower showed that jays vomit after eating one and then avoid them.

items.ask: In Ehrlich and Raven's escape and radiate, why does a plant group with a new poison split into many species?
choices: Freed from its eaters, it spreads into new places and splits into more species
The insects that eat it carry its seeds
items.why: Until an insect evolves a way through, the group loses less to eaters and can spread, so it splits into more species than its sister groups.

items.ask: Which statement about plants and the animals that eat them is best supported?
choices: Plants defend themselves, and each eater can handle only some defences
Plants are defenceless, and only predators protect them
Most leaves are left alone because insects are rare
items.why: Poisons, silica, spines and defences made on demand keep most eaters off most plants. That is one reason the world is green.

summary: **Cabbage white caterpillars eat only plants with mustard oils.** Cabbages, capers and nasturtiums share the chemistry, not the looks.
**Verschaffelt (1910) smeared mustard juice on refused leaves, and they were eaten.** The poison that keeps other insects away is the specialist's signal for food.
**Plants defend themselves.** Poisons, silica, spines and stinging hairs; some plants make more poison once bitten. Fraenkel (1959) argued this is what such chemicals are for.
**Defence costs growth.** It pays only if it saves more leaf than it costs, so the best plant is seldom the most poisonous one.
**Specialists beat one family's defences.** Then they often eat nothing else; monarchs even store the milkweed's poison against birds.
**Escape and radiate (Ehrlich and Raven, 1964).** A new poison frees a plant group from its eaters and it splits into many species, until a specialist catches up.
**The world is green partly because it is tough and poisonous.** Predators holding plant-eaters down (Ecology 8) is the other part.

talking.title: Talking trees?
talking.text: In 1983 Ian Baldwin and Jack Schultz reported that undamaged poplar and maple saplings, sharing air with torn ones, raised their own defences, and David Rhoades reported the same in willows. Newspapers wrote of talking trees. Other ecologists pointed out weaknesses in how the experiments were set up, and the idea was doubted for years. Later work, especially Richard Karban's on sagebrush from 2000 onward, showed that plants do respond to the airborne chemicals of damaged neighbours, though more weakly and less often than the first headlines suggested.

gut.title: Defusing the bomb
gut.text: When a cabbage leaf is chewed, its enzyme normally turns the glucosides into isothiocyanates, the poisonous mustard oils. In the cabbage white's gut a protein steers the same reaction to make nitriles instead, which are far less harmful. Ute Wittstock and colleagues described it in 2004, and the gene for it appears in the butterfly family at about the time the mustard-oil plants spread.

glucosinolates.title: Glucosinolates
glucosinolates.text: Verschaffelt called them mustard-oil glucosides; today's chemists call them glucosinolates, and the enzyme that splits off the sugar is myrosinase.

monarch.title: The monarch's heart
monarch.text: The milkweed's poisons, cardenolides, work like foxglove's digitalis: they jam the sodium-potassium pump that animal nerves and hearts depend on. The monarch's own pump differs by a few amino acids at the spot where the poison grips, so the poison slides off while the caterpillar stores it safely.
